voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: One snowy night in February of 1855, in the English county of Devon, something walked. By morning, a single-file trail of small hoof-shaped prints stretched for miles across the snow.

Dozens of villages reported the same tracks the same morning — as much as a hundred miles of them, all told. The prints went over rooftops. Through solid walls. Across a river. Never once doubling back.
A local vicar wrote it up for a London newspaper, and the story spread nationwide within weeks. People whispered it was the Devil himself, out walking.
Investigators proposed an escaped kangaroo. A rope of field mice. A pony's hooves, refrozen into one long unbroken line. None of it quite explained everything that was reported.
No one ever proved which theory was right — or whether the whole account grew taller in the telling. A hundred and seventy years later, the tracks in the snow are still just tracks in the snow.
